claim: Sciatic nerve crush injury triggers sterile inflammation within the distal nerve and axotomized dorsal root ganglia (DRGs).
source: Sciatic nerve crush injury triggers sterile inflammation within the distal nerve and axotomized dorsal root ganglia (DRGs).
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and RNA-seq data.

claim: Granulocytes and pro-inflammatory Ly6Chigh monocytes infiltrate the nerve first and rapidly give way to Ly6Cnegative inflammation-resolving macrophages.
source: Granulocytes and pro-inflammatory Ly6Chigh monocytes infiltrate the nerve first and rapidly give way to Ly6Cnegative inflammation-resolving macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing temporal changes in immune cell populations (Figure 1 and Figure 6).

claim: In axotomized DRGs, few hematogenous leukocytes are detected and resident macrophages acquire a ramified morphology.
source: In axotomized DRGs, few hematogenous leukocytes are detected and resident macrophages acquire a ramified morphology.
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiments (Figure 3) and whole-mount DRG imaging with morphological analysis.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing of injured sciatic nerve identifies five macrophage subpopulations, repair Schwann cells, and mesenchymal precursor cells.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing of injured sciatic nerve identifies five macrophage subpopulations, repair Schwann cells, and mesenchymal precursor cells.
evidence: This is directly supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Macrophages at the nerve crush site are molecularly distinct from macrophages associated with Wallerian degeneration.
source: Macrophages at the nerve crush site are molecularly distinct from macrophages associated with Wallerian degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis showing distinct Mac subpopulations and Arg1-YFP reporter mouse data showing spatial segregation (Figure 6).

claim: In the injured nerve, macrophages 'eat' apoptotic leukocytes, a process called efferocytosis, and thereby promote an anti-inflammatory milieu.
source: In the injured nerve, macrophages 'eat' apoptotic leukocytes, a process called efferocytosis, and thereby promote an anti-inflammatory milieu.
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiments showing CD45.1+tdTom+CD45.2- cells (Figure 7) and expression analysis of efferocytosis-related genes.

claim: Myeloid cells in the injured nerve, but not axotomized DRGs, strongly express receptors for the cytokine GM-CSF.
source: Myeloid cells in the injured nerve, but not axotomized DRGs, strongly express receptors for the cytokine GM-CSF.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data showing Csf2ra and Csf2rb expression in nerve myeloid cells (Figure 8B-C) and bulk RNA-seq of DRGs (Figure 4K-L).

claim: In GM-CSF-deficient (Csf2-/-) mice, inflammation resolution is delayed and conditioning-lesion-induced regeneration of DRG neuron central axons is abolished.
source: In GM-CSF-deficient (Csf2-/-) mice, inflammation resolution is delayed and conditioning-lesion-induced regeneration of DRG neuron central axons is abolished.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry showing altered Ly6C distribution in Csf2-/- mice (Figure 8H) and dorsal column axon tracing experiments (Figure 8J-K).

claim: Carefully orchestrated inflammation resolution in the nerve is required for conditioning-lesion-induced neurorepair.
source: Thus, carefully orchestrated inflammation resolution in the nerve is required for conditioning-lesion-induced neurorepair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Csf2-/- mouse experiments showing that perturbed inflammation resolution correlates with loss of conditioning-lesion effects.

claim: Regeneration of dorsal column axons in the rodent spinal cord can be augmented if preceded by a conditioning lesion to the sciatic nerve.
source: However, regeneration of dorsal column axons in the rodent spinal cord can be augmented if preceded by a conditioning lesion to the sciatic nerve (McQuarrie et al., 1977; Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Issa, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Traumatic PNS injury leads to sterile inflammation at the site of injury and within the distal nerve stump where axons undergo Wallerian degeneration.
source: Traumatic PNS injury leads to sterile inflammation at the site of injury and within the distal nerve stump where axons undergo Wallerian degeneration (Kim and Moalem-Taylor, 2011; Perry et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A remote inflammatory response is observed in axotomized dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) following PNS injury.
source: In addition, a remote inflammatory response is observed in axotomized dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) (Hu and McLachlan, 2003; Lu and Richardson, 1991) and the lumbar spinal cord (Guan et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The innate arm of the immune system is important for peripheral nerve regeneration, as well as conditioning-lesion-induced dorsal column axon regeneration.
source: The innate arm of the immune system is important for peripheral nerve regeneration, as well as conditioning-lesion-induced dorsal column axon regeneration (Kwon et al., 2015; Niemi et al., 2013; Salegio et al., 2011; Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Very recent studies employed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to describe gene expression in naive and injured peripheral nervous tissue at cellular resolution.
source: Very recent studies employed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to describe gene expression in naive and injured peripheral nervous tissue at cellular resolution (Wang et al., 2020; Wolbert et al., 2020; Ydens et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: A comparative analysis of immune cell profiles within the injured sciatic nerve and axotomized DRGs has not yet been carried out.
source: A comparative analysis of immune cell profiles within the injured sciatic nerve and axotomized DRGs, however, has not yet been carried out.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature that this study addresses.

claim: In naive mice, ~300 live leukocytes (CD45+) are detected within a ~ 5 mm nerve segment.
source: In naive mice, ~300 live leukocytes (CD45+) are detected within a ~ 5 mm nerve segment.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At day 1 following SNC (d1), the number of CD45+ cells in the distal nerve increases sharply, peaks around 23,100 ± 180 cells at d3, and declines to 14,000 ± 200 at d7.
source: At day 1 following SNC (d1), the number of CD45+ cells in the distal nerve increases sharply, peaks around 23,100 ± 180 cells at d3, and declines to 14,000 ± 200 at d7 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Granulocytes are absent from naive nerve, but increase to 7,800 ± 300 at d1, and by d3, the number of GC dropped below 1000.
source: Further analysis shows that granulocytes (GC), identified as CD45+CD11b+Ly6G+CD11c- cells, are absent from naive nerve, but increase to 7,800 ± 300 at d1. By d3, the number of GC dropped below 1000 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: A robust and prolonged increase of the Mo/Mac population is observed, reaching 7300 ± 120 cells at d1, peaking around 13,200 ± 240 at d3, and declining to 3200 ± 90 at d7.
source: A robust and prolonged increase of the Mo/Mac population (CD45+CD11b+Ly6G-CD11c-) is observed, reaching 7300 ± 120 cells at d1, peaking around 13,200 ± 240 at d3, and declining to 3200 ± 90 at d7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MoDC) are sparse at d1, reach 1100 ± 30 at d3, and 3400 ± 60 at d7.
source: Monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MoDC), identified as CD45+CD11b+Ly6G-CD11c+ cells, increase more gradually. They are sparse at d1, reach 1100 ± 30 at d3, and 3400 ± 60 at d7 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Few CD11b- conventional DC (cDC) are present at d1 and d3 and cDC increase to 600 ± 20 at d7.
source: Few CD11b- conventional DC (cDC), identified as CD45+CD11b-Ly6G-CD11c+ cells, are present at d1 and d3 and cDC increase to 600 ± 20 at d7 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The total number of lymphocytes is low, but significantly elevated at d1, d3, and d7 post-SNC.
source: The total number of lymphocytes (CD45+CD11b-CD11c-Ly6G-) is low, but significantly elevated at d1, d3, and d7 post-SNC (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1G and H.

claim: SNC does not significantly alter immune cells number or composition in the proximal nerve stump.
source: In marked contrast to the distal nerve stump, flow cytometry of the proximal nerve stump shows that SNC does not significantly alter immune cells number or composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–K).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SNC-elicited inflammation in the nerve is confined to the crush site and the distal nerve stump where severed fibers undergo rapid Wallerian degeneration.
source: In sum, SNC-elicited inflammation in the nerve is confined to the crush site and the distal nerve stump where severed fibers undergo rapid Wallerian degeneration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data showing spatial distribution of immune cells.

claim: SNC causes a transient increase in Iba1 and F4/80 immunolabeling in DRGs, peaking around d3 and declining at d7.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of DRG sections shows that SNC causes a transient increase in Iba1 and F4/80 immunolabeling, peaking around d3 and declining at d7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis of DRGs from naive mice identifies on average ~600 live leukocytes per ganglion.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of DRGs from naive mice identifies on average ~600 live leukocytes per ganglion, including GC, Mo/Mac, MoDC, cDC, and lymphocytes (Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2B-G.

claim: At d3 post-SNC, there is a ~ 2-fold increase in leukocytes in DRGs; however, a significant increase is only observed for Mo/Mac.
source: At d3, there is a ~ 2-fold increase in leukocytes; however, a significant increase is only observed for Mo/Mac (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: At d7 post-SNC, the Mo/Mac population in DRGs is significantly reduced compared to d3.
source: At d7, the Mo/Mac population is significantly reduced compared to d3.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The MoDC and cDC populations in DRGs are elevated at d7 when compared to DRGs from naïve mice.
source: The MoDC and cDC populations are elevated at d7 when compared to DRGs from naïve mice (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Lymphocytes are present in naive DRGs but do not significantly increase during the first week post-SNC.
source: Lymphocytes are present in naive DRGs but do not significantly increase during the first week post-SNC (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Western blotting shows that the injury induced increase in myeloid cells in the nerve trunk exceeds the one in axotomized DRGs by an order of magnitude.
source: Probing tissue lysates with anti-CD11b shows that the injury induced increase in myeloid cells in the nerve trunk exceeds the one in axotomized DRGs by an order of magnitude (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 2H and I.

claim: SNC induces a remote immune response in axotomized DRGs that is strikingly different in magnitude and cellular composition from injured nerve tissue.
source: Taken together, these studies show that SNC induces a remote immune response in axotomized DRGs that is strikingly different in magnitude and cellular composition from injured nerve tissue.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative flow cytometry and Western blot data from nerves and DRGs.

claim: One month after parabiosis surgery, myeloid cell chimerism in the spleen is 27.3 ± 1.5%.
source: Shared blood circulation was assessed by flow cytometry of the spleen, and revealed a myeloid cell (CD45+CD11b+) chimerism of 27.3 ± 1.5 (gating strategy is illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from parabiotic mice.

claim: At d3 following SNC, 28.4 ± 6.7% of myeloid cells in nerves from WT parabionts are tdTom+.
source: At d3 following SNC, flow cytometric analysis of nerves isolated from WT parabionts identifies 28.4 ± 6.7% tdTom+ myeloid (CD45+CD11b+) cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from parabiotic mice presented in Figure 3B.

claim: 27.1 ± 6.9% of Mo/Mac and 30 ± 5.6% of MoDC in the injured WT parabiont nerve are tdTom+.
source: Fractionation of myeloid cells into Mo/Mac (CD45+CD11b+Ly6G-CD11c-) and MoDC (CD45+CD11b+Ly6G-CD11c+) further revealed that 27.1 ± 6.9% of Mo/Mac and 30 ± 5.6% of MoDC are tdTom+ in the injured WT parabiont (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from parabiotic mice presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Blood-borne cells make up the vast majority of immune cells in the injured nerve.
source: When coupled with ~27% chimerism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), this suggests that blood-borne cells make up the vast majority of immune cells in the injured nerve.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chimerism data and the percentage of tdTom+ cells in the injured nerve.

claim: At d3 and d7 post-SNC, tdTom+ cells are preferentially found at the injury site but also present within the distal nerve stump.
source: At d3 and d7, tdTom+ cells are preferentially found at the injury site but also present within the distal nerve stump where fibers undergo Wallerian degeneration (Figure 3D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the proximal nerve, very few tdTom+ cells are detected at any post-SNC time point.
source: In the proximal nerve, very few tdTom+ cells are detected at any post-SNC time point (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Following SNC, there is a modest, but statistically significant increase in tdTom+ cells in DRGs at d3 and d7, but not at 14 days.
source: Following SNC, there is a modest, but statistically significant increase in tdTom+ cells at d3 and d7, but not at 14 days, suggesting that only a small number of hematogenous leukocytes enter axotomized DRGs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of tdTom+ cells in DRG sections presented in Figure 3F.

claim: SNC-elicited intra-ganglionic increase of Iba1+ and F4/80+ immune profiles primarily occurs through mechanisms that involve DRG-resident macrophages, rather than hematogenous immune cells.
source: Together these studies show that SNC-elicited intra-ganglionic increase of Iba1+ and F4/80+ immune profiles (Figure 2A) primarily occurs through mechanisms that involve DRG-resident macrophages, rather than hematogenous immune cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the parabiosis data showing limited infiltration of tdTom+ cells into DRGs.

claim: During the first 2 weeks post-SNC, no tdTom+ cells were detected in the lumbar spinal cord.
source: Of note, during the first 2 weeks post-SNC, no tdTom+ cells were detected in the lumbar spinal cord (data not shown), suggesting that hematogenous immune cells do not significantly contribute to SNC-triggered spinal cord inflammation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the parabiosis experiments.

claim: Three-dimensional projection analysis of Mac profiles in DRGs reveals a 2.3-fold increase in the total volume occupied by Iba1+ cells at 3 days post-SNC.
source: Three-dimensional projection analysis of Mac profiles, in the absence of nerve injury (intact) and at 3 days post-SNC, revealed a 2.3-fold increase in the total volume occupied by Iba1+ cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantification of Iba1+ cells in whole-mount DRGs presented in Figure 3I.

claim: In intact DRGs, 84 ± 2% of macrophages have amoeboid morphology and 16 ± 2% have elongated morphology.
source: Two distinct Mac morphologies were observed in intact DRGs, a majority (84 ± 2%) of amoeboid cells and a smaller population (16 ± 2%) of elongated cells (Figure 3H and J).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis of Iba1+ cells in whole-mount DRGs presented in Figure 3H and J.

claim: At d3 post-SNC, macrophages in DRGs exhibit amoeboid (60 ± 2%), elongated (10 ± 3%), and stellate (30 ± 4%) morphologies.
source: At d3, Mac with amoeboid (60 ± 2%), elongated (10 ± 3%), and stellate morphologies (30 ± 4%) are identified.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis presented in Figure 3J.

claim: At d7 post-SNC, macrophages in DRGs exhibit amoeboid (40 ± 3%), elongated (5 ± 1%), and stellate (55 ± 4%) morphologies.
source: And at d7, amoeboid (40 ± 3%), elongated (5 ± 1%), and stellate (55 ± 4%) shaped Mac are detected (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis presented in Figure 3J.

claim: SNC-triggered Mac morphological changes do not alter the average volume of individual cells.
source: While the SNC-triggered Mac morphological changes are quite striking, they do not alter the average volume of individual cells (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell volumes presented in Figure 3K.

claim: Local proliferation and morphological changes, rather than infiltration of blood-borne cells, contribute to increased Iba1 immunoreactivity in axotomized DRGs.
source: Based on these studies, we conclude that local proliferation and morphological changes, rather than infiltration of blood-borne cells, contribute to increased Iba1 immunoreactivity in axotomized DRGs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the parabiosis data and morphological analysis of DRG macrophages.

claim: WGCNA identifies a pink module enriched for regeneration associated gene (RAG) products, including Jun, Fos, Stat3, Smad1, Atf3.
source: Focusing on prominently regulated gene modules, we find a previously described module (pink module [Chandran et al., 2016]), enriched for regeneration associated gene (RAG) products, including Jun, Fos, Stat3, Smad1, Atf3, among other genes.
evidence: This is supported by WGCNA analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from DRGs, with citation to previous work.

claim: WGCNA identifies a large turquoise module that is stably upregulated following SNC and enriched for immune system processes.
source: In addition, WGCNA identifies a large turquoise module (Figure 4A and B), which along with the pink module, is stably upregulated following SNC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B). To annotate module function, we applied gene ontology (GO) enrichment analyses, which showed enrichment (Benjamini-corrected p values < 0.05) for several GO categories associated with immune system function in the turquoise module.
evidence: This is supported by WGCNA and GO enrichment analysis presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most significantly upregulated GO terms in the turquoise module include cell activation, immune effector process, and defense response.
source: The most significantly upregulated GO terms include cell activation, immune effector process, and defense response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis identified several upstream activators in axotomized DRGs, including cytokines and growth factors (IFNγ, TNF, IL1b, IL6, TGFβ1, IL10, IL4, IFNβ1, IL2) and transcription regulators STAT1, STAT3, IRF7, RELA.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) identified several upstream activators, including cytokines and growth factors (IFNγ, TNF, IL1b, IL6, TGFβ1, IL10, IL4, IFNβ1, IL2) and the transcription regulators STAT1, STAT3, IRF7, RELA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The upregulation of immune system processes in axotomized DRGs correlates with a modest ~1.5-fold increase of gene products encoding the canonical macrophage markers Itgam (CD11b), Aif1 (Iba1), and Adgre1 (F4/80).
source: The upregulation of immune system processes in axotomized DRGs correlates with a modest ~1.5-fold increase of gene products encoding the canonical macrophage markers Itgam (CD11b), Aif1 (Iba1), and Adgre1 (F4/80) (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Expression levels and fold-upregulation of Atf3, Jun, and Stat3 in axotomized DRGs are very robust.
source: In comparison, expression levels and fold-upregulation of Atf3, Jun, and Stat3 are very robust (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Expression of Ccr2, Csf2ra and Csf2rb is elevated in axotomized DRGs; however, expression levels are low, especially for Csf2rb (~1 fpkm).
source: Expression of the chemokine receptor Ccr2 and the receptor subunits for the GM-CSF receptor (Csf2ra and Csf2rb) are elevated in axotomized DRGs; however, expression levels are low, especially for Csf2rb (~1 fpkm) (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Some of the immune gene activity observed in axotomized DRGs may involve non-hematopoietic cells.
source: Moreover, some of the immune gene activity observed in axotomized DRGs may involve non-hematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that immune gene expression is elevated but macrophage markers are only modestly increased.

claim: A total of 17,384 cells was sequenced from 3d injured sciatic nerves with 16,204 used for downstream analysis after quality control filtering.
source: A total of 17,384 cells was sequenced with 16,204 used for downstream analysis after removing cells with fewer than 200 genes, more than 7500, or mitochondrial content greater than 25%.
evidence: This is a description of the scRNA-seq experimental procedure and data processing.

claim: Median unique genes per cell in the scRNA-seq dataset was 2507.
source: Median unique genes per cell was 2507.
evidence: This is a quality metric for the scRNA-seq data.

claim: More than 20 different cell clusters were identified in the injured sciatic nerve using shared nearest neighbor clustering algorithm.
source: More than 20 different cell clusters were identified using shared nearest neighbor clustering algorithm.
evidence: This is a description of the computational analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Innate immune cells (Itgam/CD11b) make up a median 42.22% (±1.39%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: Innate immune cells (Itgam/CD11b) make up a median 42.22% (±1.39%), and lymphocytes less than 1.73%(±. 27%), of the cells in the injured nerve (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Lymphocytes make up less than 1.73% (±0.27%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: Innate immune cells (Itgam/CD11b) make up a median 42.22% (±1.39%), and lymphocytes less than 1.73%(±. 27%), of the cells in the injured nerve (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Three distinct MES subpopulations are identified in the injured sciatic nerve.
source: We identify three distinct MES subpopulations (Figure 5A), reminiscent of a recent study examining the nerve response to digit tip amputation (Carr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis presented in Figure 5A, with citation to related work.

claim: MES make up 18.49% (±0.98%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: In the injured sciatic nerve, MES make up 18.49% (±0.98%) of cells and differentially express the markers Pdfgra and Sox9 (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: MES are a rich source of extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules, including collagens, fibronectin, fibrillin-1, laminin-b2, and numerous proteoglycans.
source: MES are a rich source of extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules, including collagens (Col1a, Col3a, Col5a, Col6a), Fn1/fibronectin, Fbn1/fibrillin-1, Lamb2/laminin-b2, and numerous proteoglycans (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Individual MES clusters are identified as perineural MES (pMES), endoneurial MES (eMES), and differentiating MES (dMES) based on marker gene expression.
source: Individual MES clusters are identified as perineural MES (pMES) (Slc2a1/Glut1, Itgb4/integrin-β4, Stra6/stimulated by retinoic acid 6, Sfrp5/secreted frizzled related protein 5), endoneurial MES (eMES) (Wif1/Wnt inhibitory factor 1, Bmp7), and differentiating MES (dMES) (Gas1/Growth arrest-specific 1, Ly6a/SCA-1, Tnc/tenascin, Sfrp1/secreted frizzled-related protein 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq marker gene expression analysis.

claim: STRING Reactome pathway analysis for MES clusters identifies extracellular matrix organization as top hit.
source: STRING Reactome pathway analysis for MES clusters identifies extracellular matrix organization as top hit (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells in eMES, but not in clusters pMES and dMES, are neural crest derived.
source: Further analysis revealed that cells in eMES, but not in clusters pMES and dMES, are neural crest derived (Carr et al., 2019; Gugala et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural crest markers, with citations to related work.

claim: Three clusters of Schwann cells (SC1-3) represent 17.48% (±1.53%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: Three clusters of Schwann cells (SC1-3) represent 17.48% (±1.53%) of cells in the injured nerve (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Cluster SC1 contains proliferating cells marked by Mki67/Ki67 expression.
source: Cluster SC1 contains proliferating cells marked by Mki67/Ki67 expression (Figure 5J) and many cells that strongly express Ncam1, Chl1/cell adhesion molecule L1-like, Erbb3, Epha5, Thbs2/thrombospondin-2, Tnc, Hbegf, and the BMP antagonist Sostdc1 (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: SC1 enriched transcription regulators include Zfp706, Tead1, Sox6, Nr2f1/COUP-TF.
source: SC1 enriched transcription regulators (SC1-TR) include Zfp706, Tead1, Sox6, Nr2f1/COUP-TF (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5K.

claim: SC3 cells express high levels of Ngfr/p75, Nrcam, Gfra1, Btc, Gjb1, Cryab, Tnfrsf12a, Gadd45b.
source: SC3 cells express high levels of Ngfr/p75, Nrcam, Gfra1/GDNF family receptor alpha 1, Btc/betacellulin, Gjb1/connexin-32, Cryab/crystallin alpha B, Tnfrsf12a/Fn14, Gadd45b (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: SC3-TR include Sox4, Runx2, Hmga1, Jun, and Pou3f1.
source: SC3-TR include Sox4, Runx2, Hmga1, Jun, and the POU family member Pou3f1, a repressor of BMP and Wnt signaling, associated with a pro-myelinating cell state (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5K.

claim: Cluster SC2 expresses nes/nestin and Cryab.
source: Cluster SC2, flanked by SC1 and SC3, expresses nes/nestin and Cryab.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: STRING identified axon guidance and integrin cell surface interactions as top REACTOME pathways for SC1.
source: STRING identified axon guidance and integrin cell surface interactions as top REACTOME pathways for SC1.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Axon guidance, gap junction assembly, and microtubule-dependent trafficking are top hits for SC3.
source: Axon guidance, gap junction assembly, and microtubule-dependent trafficking are top hits for SC3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells associated with the nerve vasculature make up 14.2% (±3.19%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: Cells associated with the nerve vasculature make up 14.2% (±3.19%).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Three clusters of endothelial cells (EC1-3) represent 9.92% (±2.69%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: They include three clusters of endothelial cells (EC1-3), strongly expressing Pecam/CD31, representing 9.92% (±2.69%) of cells (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Two pericyte cell clusters (PC1 and PC2) represent 4.2% (±0.44%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: There are two pericyte cell clusters (PC1 and PC2) enriched for the pericyte markers (Pdgfrb, Rgs5) and vasculature-associated smooth muscle cells (Acta2, Des, Myl9, Mylk), representing 4.2% (±. 44%) (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: A small cluster of chondrocyte-like cells (CL) represents 0.5% (±0.44%) of cells in the injured nerve.
source: A small cluster of chondrocyte-like cells (CL: Comp/cartilage oligomeric matrix protein, Col27a1, Jun) represents 0.5% (±0.44%).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: MES and Fb are rich sources of gene products with neurotrophic and neurotropic properties.
source: MES and Fb are rich sources of gene products with neurotrophic and neurotropic properties, and thus may act in a paracrine fashion to regulate neuronal survival and direct axonal growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: dMES express Igf1, Ogn, Nid1, Ntn1, Postn, Gdf10, Cxcl12, Dcn, Grn, Sparc, Lamb2, Serpinf1.

source: AC are selectively recognized due to phosphatidylserine (PS) or calreticulin (Calr) accumulation on their surface; both function as strong 'eat me' signals (Figure 7A).
